title: Estimating an unknown quantity
objectives: Give a fair value and a range for a quantity you cannot look up.

screens.title: The opener
screens.prose: The interviewer says: make me a market on the digits needed to number the pages of a 300-page book. Do not calculate yet. Drag the dot to your best guess, and the two ends to a range you are 90% sure of.

derive.caption: Your guess {{fv.x}}, your range {{min(lo.x, hi.x)}} to {{max(lo.x, hi.x)}}

screens.question: Before any working, what does your range claim?

options.text: If I made many ranges like this, about 9 in 10 would hold the true count.
The count is certainly between my two ends.
options.why: You read 90% as certainty. A 90% range is allowed to miss about 1 time in 10.

options.text: The count is most likely near one of the two ends.
options.why: The ends mark where surprise begins. The count is most likely near your guess in the middle.

options.text: My guess is right to the nearest page.
options.why: Nobody can guess to the page before working it out. The range says how far off you might be.

hints.text: Ninety per cent is not one hundred per cent.
Think of ten different questions, each answered with a range like this one.
About nine of ten such ranges should hold the truth, and one should miss.

feedback.correct: Correct. A 90% range should miss about once in ten.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. A 90% range is a claim about how often ranges like it hold the truth.

explain.text: Your dot is a point estimate: the centre of what you believe. The range is its spread, wide enough that you would be surprised 1 time in 10. Next we work out the count and test your range.

screens.title: Now work it out
screens.prose: You gave a **fair value**, your single best guess, and a **range** around it. Now the count itself. Pages 1 to 9 use one digit each, 10 to 99 use two, and 100 to 300 use three.

state.caption: Where does the true count sit?

screens.question: Fill in the table.

hints.text: How many whole numbers run from 100 to 300, counting both ends?
Two-digit pages: 10 to 99 is 90 pages, each with 2 digits.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the pages in each block, both ends included, then multiply by the digits each page uses.

byKey.r1c2: Pages 10 to 99 are 90 pages of 2 digits each: 180.
byKey.r2c1: From 100 to 300 inclusive is 300 − 100 + 1 = 201 pages. Subtracting alone drops page 100.
byKey.r2c2: Each of the 201 three-digit pages uses 3 digits: 603. If you wrote 600, you dropped page 100.
byKey.r3c2: Add the three blocks: 9 + 180 + 603. If you wrote 900, you gave every page three digits.

explain.text: One-digit pages give 9, two-digit pages give 180, and the 201 three-digit pages give 603. The total is 792. Check it against the range you dragged a moment ago.

screens.title: Squares on a chessboard
screens.prose: Next question in the round: how many squares of any size are on a chessboard? Say a fair value and a range first. Then count. A $k$ by $k$ square can start in $9 - k$ columns and $9 - k$ rows.

state.caption: One 3 by 3 square. It can start in 6 columns and 6 rows.

screens.question: Fill in the counts.

hints.text: Slide the shaded 3 by 3 square right. How many places can it start in one row?
It can start in columns 1 to 6, and in rows 1 to 6.
Each size $k$ gives $(9-k)^2$ squares: 64, 49, 36, 25, 16, 9, 4, 1. They add to 204.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each size $k$ gives $(9-k)^2$ squares. Add all eight sizes.

byKey.r2c1: Count where a 3 by 3 square can start: 6 places across and 6 down. If you wrote 9, you counted the cells inside one.
byKey.r7c1: The 8 by 8 square is the whole board, and it fits in exactly one place.
byKey.r8c1: Add all eight sizes. If you wrote 64 or 65, you left out the middle sizes.

explain.text: A 3 by 3 square can start in 6 places across and 6 down, so 36 of them. The sizes give 64, 49, 36, 25, 16, 9, 4 and 1, which add to 204. Counting only the smallest squares gives 64, or 65 with the whole board, well below the truth.

canvas.caption: 6 starting columns and 6 starting rows: 36 squares of size 3

screens.title: Ten ranges
screens.prose: A candidate gave these ten 90% ranges in a practice round. Each truth is exact, so every range can be marked.

state.caption: Ten 90% ranges and the truths (m is a million)

screens.question: Tap every row whose range missed the truth.

hints.text: For each row, is the truth at least Low and at most High?
Row 2: the truth, 204, is above the high end, 150.
Three rows miss: the chessboard squares, the card hands and the rectangles.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. A range misses when the truth is below Low or above High.

byKey.two-only: You missed one. The rectangles, 1,296, sit above the high end of 1,000.
byKey.two-only-b: You missed one. The card hands, 2,598,960, sit above the high end of 1,000,000.
byKey.r0: 792 lies between 500 and 900, so that range held.
byKey.r2: 31,536,000 lies between 30 and 35 million, so that range held.
byKey.r3: 10,080 lies between 8,000 and 12,000, so that range held.
byKey.r4: 8,784 lies between 8,000 and 9,000, so that range held.
byKey.r6: 40,320 lies between 1,000 and 50,000, so that range held.
byKey.r7: 2,893 lies between 2,500 and 3,500, so that range held.
byKey.r8: 435 lies between 400 and 500, so that range held.

explain.text: Three truths fall outside their ranges: 204, 2,598,960 and 1,296. Every miss sits above the high end. The candidate guessed low on counting questions.

screens.title: The hit rate
screens.prose: The same ten ranges. The share of ranges that hold the truth is the **hit rate**. For 90% ranges it should be close to 0.9.

state.caption: Three of the ten ranges missed

screens.question: What is this candidate’s hit rate?

widget.accept: 0.7, or 7/10: seven of the ten ranges held the truth.
widget.label: Hit rate as a decimal

hints.text: Count the rows that held, not the rows that missed.
Seven rows held the truth.
Hit rate = 7 / 10.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide the ranges that held the truth by all ten.

byKey.misses: That is the miss rate, 3 in 10. The hit rate counts the ranges that held.
byKey.count: That is the number of hits. Divide by the ten ranges to get a rate.

explain.text: Seven of ten ranges held the truth, a hit rate of 0.7 against the 0.9 promised. A calibrated forecaster scores 7 or fewer only about 7% of the time. That is a warning, not proof: the ranges look too narrow, which is overconfidence.

screens.title: Too narrow, too wide
screens.prose: The interviewer asks for the hours in a leap year, and a 90% range before you calculate. Three candidates answer. A says 8,700 to 8,710. B says 0 to 100,000. C says 8,000 to 9,500.

state.caption: Three 90% ranges. B runs off both ends of the axis.

screens.question: Which answer would the interviewer accept?

options.text: A: 8,700 to 8,710, because it is precise.
options.why: You chose a 10-hour range on a guess. It looks precise, but it misses the true 8,784.

options.text: B: 0 to 100,000, because it cannot miss.
options.why: You chose a range that cannot miss, so it says nothing. The interviewer will call it useless.

options.text: C: 8,000 to 9,500, from 365 × 24 with room to spare.

options.why: You gave zero width before checking the leap day. A leap year has 366 days, so 8,784 hours.

hints.text: A useful range is neither a guess with decimals nor everything.
Start from 365 × 24 = 8,760 and ask how wrong that could be.
C is centred near 8,760 and wide enough to survive a slip. The truth is 366 × 24 = 8,784.

feedback.correct: C is centred on a reason and wide enough to be honest.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Pick the range that is narrow enough to be useful and wide enough to be honest.

byKey.narrow: You chose a 10-hour range on a guess. It is overconfident: it misses the true 8,784.
byKey.wide: You chose a range that cannot miss. It is safe and useless: it tells the interviewer nothing.

explain.text: C starts from 365 × 24 = 8,760 and leaves room for a slip. The truth is 366 × 24 = 8,784, inside C and outside A. B always holds the truth and never helps anyone.

screens.title: A number you know
screens.prose: Next the interviewer asks for a market on the minutes in a week. You can work it out in your head: $7 \times 24 \times 60 = 10{,}080$.
screens.question: What range do you give now?

options.text: 10,080 to 10,080, and say the number is exact.
10,000 to 10,200, to be safe.
options.why: You put a range round a number you have already worked out. A range is for what you do not know.

options.text: Refuse to quote, because there is nothing to trade.
options.why: The interviewer still wants an answer. Say you know it exactly and quote it with zero width.

options.text: 9,000 to 11,000, the usual 10% either side.
options.why: There is no usual width. Width comes from your uncertainty, and here you have none.

hints.text: How unsure are you, after the multiplication?
Width should match uncertainty.
The number is known, so the range has zero width: 10,080 to 10,080.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask how much doubt is left once you have multiplied it out.

explain.text: Once you have multiplied it out there is no doubt left, so the range has zero width. Say so aloud: the interviewer is checking that width follows uncertainty. A padded range here would show the opposite.

screens.title: Calibration
screens.prose: You scored ten ranges by their hits. You are **calibrated** when your ranges at level $p$ hold the truth a share $p$ of the time. $$\text{hit rate} = \frac{\text{number of } i \text{ with } L_i \le x_i \le H_i}{n} \approx p.$$ The fair value is the centre of a belief, and the range is its spread.
screens.question: You give 20 calibrated 90% ranges. About how many should miss?

widget.accept: 2: a 90% range misses 10% of the time, and 10% of 20 is 2.
widget.label: Ranges that miss

feedback.generic: Not quite right. A 90% range misses 10% of the time.

byKey.hits: That is the number that should hold the truth. The question asks for the misses.
byKey.none: Calibrated 90% ranges still miss about 1 time in 10. Never missing means the ranges are too wide.

explain.text: A 90% range misses 10% of the time, so about 2 of 20 should miss. Missing none is a warning too: the ranges are wider than they need to be. Zero misses in 20 happens by chance only about 12% of the time.

screens.title: Any book
screens.prose: Back to the book. For any three-digit page count $n$, pages 1 to 99 always use $9 + 180 = 189$ digits. The pages from 100 to $n$ use three each.
screens.question: Write the digits needed to number pages 1 to $n$, for $100 \le n \le 999$.

hints.text: How many pages run from 100 to $n$, both ends included?
There are $n - 99$ three-digit pages.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add 189 to three times the number of pages from 100 to $n$.

byKey.fence: You used $n - 100$ three-digit pages. From 100 to $n$ inclusive there are $n - 99$.
byKey.no-short: That gives every page three digits. Pages 1 to 99 use only 189 digits, not 297.

explain.text: Pages 100 to $n$ number $n - 99$, each with three digits. So the total is $189 + 3(n - 99) = 3n - 108$. At $n = 300$ that is 792, as you counted.

screens.title: Check it in code
screens.prose: Put both checks in code, so you can score any practice round. A range holds its truth when low ≤ truth ≤ high.
screens.question: Complete `digits_to_number(n)` and `calibration(intervals, truths)`.

widget.how: Check runs 10 hidden tests. Digit counts must be exact; each hit rate must be within a relative 1e-9 of the exact share.

hints.text: Work in blocks: 1 to 9, 10 to 99, 100 to 999, and so on.
A block of $d$-digit pages runs from $10^{d-1}$ to $10^d - 1$, cut off at $n$.
For calibration, count `lo <= t <= hi` over `zip(intervals, truths)` and divide by the number of truths.

feedback.generic: Some tests failed. Check both ends of each page block, and count a truth equal to an end as a hit.

byKey.error: Your code stopped with an error. Check that each `...` is replaced.

explain.text:
Each block of $d$-digit pages adds (pages in block) × $d$, with the last block cut at $n$. `calibration` counts `lo <= t <= hi`, so a truth on an end is a hit. On the practice round it returns 7/10.

```python
hits = sum(lo <= t <= hi for (lo, hi), t in zip(intervals, truths))
```

screens.title: The interviewer trades
screens.prose: The interviewer asks your price to sell one contract that pays £1 per digit in the 300-page book. You say £850. They buy one from you. The contract settles at the true count.
screens.question: What is your P&L on the trade, in pounds?

widget.accept: £58: you sold at £850 a contract worth £792.
widget.label: P&L in pounds

hints.text: You received £850. What do you pay out at settlement?
You are short one contract, so you pay its value, £792.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. You received the price and pay out the true count.

byKey.sign: You sold above the value, so you gain. A seller makes price minus value: 850 − 792.
byKey.price: That is the cash you received. You also pay out £792 when it settles.

explain.text: You took £850 and pay out £792 at settlement, so you make £58. A sell price below the true value would have lost, so you ask more than your fair value. Here your price was 58 above the truth, so the trade went your way.

screens.title: The first 30 seconds
screens.prose: A trader interview opens: "Make me a market on the digits in a 300-page book." The interviewer marks the reasoning as it happens. *Probability and Markets*, a free guide written by a trading firm, describes rounds like this.

state.caption: Say the number, the range and why

screens.question: Which opening is best?

options.text: "About 800, between 600 and 1,000: roughly 300 pages of 3 digits, less the short early pages."
Thirty seconds of silent working, then "792."
options.why: You gave the answer with no range and no reasoning. The interviewer marks how you get there, and silence scores nothing.

options.text: "Somewhere between 1 and 10,000."
options.why: You chose a range that cannot miss. It says nothing, so the interviewer will push you to narrow it.

options.text: "Exactly 900, since each page has 3 digits."
options.why: You gave false precision and a slip: pages 1 to 99 use fewer than 3 digits each.

hints.text: The interviewer wants three things: a number, a range and a reason.
Only one answer gives all three.
About 800, from 300 × 3 less the short pages, with a range of 600 to 1,000.

feedback.correct: A number, a range and a reason, all aloud.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Say a number, a range and the reason for both.

explain.text: The best opening says a fair value, a range and the reason, before any exact working. Then you calculate aloud and land on 792, inside the range you gave. Zhou’s green book and Crack’s *Heard on the Street* collect many more openers like this.

ideas: A fair value is the centre of your belief; a range is its spread, said before any exact working.
Calibrated 90% ranges hold the truth about 9 times in 10: score them by their hit rate.
Width follows uncertainty: a known number gets zero width, and a guess never gets a 10-hour range.
summary.trap: A range so narrow it is a guess with decimals, or so wide it says nothing.

quiz.prose: The interviewer asks for the digits needed to number a 500-page book.
quiz.question: How many digits?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the one-, two- and three-digit pages separately.

byKey.fence: You used 400 three-digit pages. Pages 100 to 500 inclusive are 401.
byKey.all-three: You gave every page three digits. Pages 1 to 99 use only 189.

explain.text: Pages 1 to 99 use 189 digits and pages 100 to 500 are 401 pages of three digits, 1,203. The total is 1,392. The formula $3n - 108$ gives the same.

quiz.prose: A trainee’s 90% ranges held the truth 12 times in 20.
quiz.question: What should the trainee change?

options.text: Widen the ranges: they are overconfident.
Narrow the ranges: they are too cautious.
options.why: You read too few hits as too much caution. Missing 8 in 20 means the ranges were too narrow.

options.text: Nothing: 12 in 20 is close to 90%.
options.why: You compared loosely. 12 in 20 is 60%, far below the 90% claimed.

options.text: Move every centre up.
options.why: Misses can fall on either side. A hit rate tells you about width, not direction.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the hit rate, 12/20, with 0.9.

explain.text: A hit rate of 12/20 = 0.6 is far below the 0.9 claimed. The ranges were too narrow, which is overconfidence. Widening them is the fix.

quiz.prose: The interviewer moves to a 4 by 4 board.
quiz.question: How many squares of any size are on it?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. A $k$ by $k$ square can start in $5 - k$ places each way.

byKey.unit-only: You counted only the 1 by 1 squares.
byKey.plus-one: You added the whole board but left out the 2 by 2 and 3 by 3 squares.

explain.text: Sizes 1 to 4 give $4^2$, $3^2$, $2^2$ and $1^2$ squares. That is 16 + 9 + 4 + 1 = 30.

quiz.prose: Your 90% range for the seconds in a 365-day year was 30 million to 35 million.
quiz.question: How many seconds are there in a 365-day year?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply days, hours, minutes and seconds.

byKey.leap: That uses 366 days. The question says 365.
byKey.minutes: That is the minutes in a year. Multiply by 60 once more.

explain.text: 365 × 24 = 8,760 hours, × 60 = 525,600 minutes, × 60 = 31,536,000 seconds. It sits inside 30 to 35 million, so that range was a hit.
